When Sophie walked in at 3:47—thirteen minutes late—she was holding her phone and frowning at the screen. Maxime's chest did something complicated. She spotted him, and her face changed, and she crossed the room with her jacket half-open, apologizing before she'd even sat down. "I got lost in the parking garage," she said. She laughed at herself, and Maxime felt something in him relax.

She was working on a series of posters for the environmental club, the kind meant to be printed and wheat-pasted around campus come fall. Her first draft showed a forest canopy, dense and intricate, with the phrase "What We Stand to Lose" arcing across the top.

She had been designing for three weeks when she discovered the image database. It was simple enough—a creative commons repository where artists uploaded photographs for others to use. She found a perfect photograph of an old-growth forest, the kind of saturated green that made her chest tighten. She could trace elements of it, or scan it and adapt it, or simply use it as reference while drawing. The photographer's name was there, a link to her website. Everything seemed legitimate and aboveboard.

But then Lea made the mistake of looking at the analytics. She had created a design account to track when her posters got printed and posted, and embedded in the platform's statistics was a small note: images that appeared online, even in protected spaces, accrued measurable value. Not in money—not directly. But in attention. Every download, every view, every time someone shared the image, the system recorded it. The photograph she had found, she learned, had been downloaded forty-seven thousand times. The photographer's work had spread across the internet in ways she herself could never have orchestrated. And yet when Lea looked at her portfolio site, it seemed barely maintained. There were no recent posts. No indication that this flood of attention had resulted in paid work.

Lea set down her pencil. She thought about the purpose of the posters—to make people care enough to act. To create something that would move through the world and do work for its own sake, for the environment's sake, not for credit or compensation. But she also thought about the photographer, whose beautiful image had become distributed labor, uncompensated attention flowing into systems that quantified and monetized what it could detect.

She opened her sketchbook to a new page. This time, instead of tracing or adapting, she drew from scratch. It took longer. The forest emerged line by line from her own hand, less photorealistic but somehow more insistent—the trees were thick and dark, almost oppressive in their repetition. It wasn't derivative. It was hers, and it was honest about its limitations. But as she worked, she realized something: the photograph had been better. More powerful. More likely to make someone stop and truly see.

By evening, Lea had two versions. In one, she had credited the photographer prominently, made a link in the digital version of the poster. In the other, she used her own drawing. She photographed both and sent them to the environmental club's coordinator with a question: which mattered more, impact or attribution? Could she use the stronger image if she made the source clear? Did clarity of source matter when the image would be printed and posted, possibly shared again without the credit attached?

The coordinator hadn't responded yet. Lea gathered her materials slowly, returning each pencil to its box. She realized she didn't yet know the answer—not the moral one, and not the practical one either. She knew only that mankind had built systems that could spread an image to forty-seven thousand people without those people ever knowing who made it, and that this was neither entirely wrong nor entirely right. She tucked her sketchbook under her arm, leaving both versions on the table to decide between them later, or perhaps to decide that some choices refused neat resolution.

Her father worked in manufacturing, had for thirty years. Every few months now came the news of reduced hours, restructured departments, positions eliminated. Her mother, always steady, had started taking extra shifts at the hospital. Lily understood that their worry had weight, real weight, but she'd never quite understood the shape of it. Not until she'd registered for her college courses and chosen environmental science as her focus, and her professor had assigned a paper on supply chains.

She'd come to the library to research, thinking she'd find numbers and diagrams. Instead, she found herself reading about automation in factories, about how a single facility could produce five times what it once did with half the workers. The technology itself wasn't new, but something in the way the economist framed it unsettled her. Increased efficiency meant decreased labor costs meant competitive advantage. She could trace it like a line on a graph: the better the machines, the fewer people needed. The fewer people needed, the lower the wages had to go to stay competitive. Her father's hours weren't being cut randomly. They were a consequence of systems optimizing themselves, each business making rational decisions that somehow added up to something her family had to survive.

A girl sat down two tables over, backpack slung onto the surface with the haste of someone running late. She opened a laptop and immediately pulled up a food delivery app, scrolling through restaurants with the furious efficiency of someone hungry and in a hurry. Lily watched her order Thai food to be delivered in twelve minutes. Twelve minutes. The girl barely glanced at the driver rating, just tapped confirm and closed the app.

Lily had used those apps a hundred times, appreciated them without thinking much about it. But now she found herself wondering who was delivering the food, whether they had benefits, whether they were liable to injury without insurance, whether this miraculous speed was actually miraculous or whether it just moved the cost somewhere else. She opened her phone and looked up the delivery company's quarterly earnings. Revenue was soaring. Driver satisfaction was not mentioned in the results.

She thought about her own summer job at a coffee shop, how the schedule changed weekly based on a software algorithm designed to minimize labor costs while maximizing coverage. She'd been liable to get called in on short notice or sent home early, making it nearly impossible to plan anything beyond a few days ahead. It had felt like the system was capricious until she realized it wasn't capricious at all. It was perfectly logical, perfectly efficient, and perfectly indifferent to whether she could afford bus fare to get to the next shift.

But here was what complicated everything: she'd bought her laptop on that same system, ordered her textbooks through it, and just this morning she'd used it to find her family a lower insurance rate. The efficiency had real benefits too. She wasn't going to pretend otherwise. The Thai food girl would eat lunch on time because of those same algorithmic optimizations. Her father's company had invested in new machinery because staying competitive meant survival. You couldn't just opt out and pretend the system didn't exist.

Lily returned to her economics textbook and actually opened it this time, but now she was reading differently, looking for something beyond what the author asserted. She found a footnote about externalities, about costs that didn't appear on a balance sheet, about the gap between what a system optimized itself toward and what actually mattered to the people inside it. She scribbled a note: *Who bears the cost of speed?* And beneath it: *How do you build something faster without asking who pays?*

The Thai food girl was on her phone now, leaving a generous tip and a kind comment about the driver being friendly. Small kindness inserted into a system that didn't require it. Her father had always said the same thing about his coworkers, how they looked out for each other on the line, how they'd cover someone's shift if their kid was sick. Goodness lived alongside the machinery. Both things were true.

The only honest place to start was admitting that contradiction, holding it without flinching.

She noticed he kept his notebook open to a blank page, never actually writing anything down, just staring at it. When she asked what he was doing, he looked up startled, as if she'd caught him doing something illicit. "Trying to figure out how to take notes," he said. "My English teacher last year kept saying I wasn't 'engaging deeply with the text.' I've been staring at strategies online all summer and none of them work."

Isla found this hilarious, which probably wasn't kind, but she laughed anyway. "You know you have to actually write something first before you can know it doesn't work, right?" She pulled out her own notebook, which was covered in doodles from August. "I just write things down and then later I have no idea what ten-year-old Isla meant by 'chaotic neutral energy,' but at least I have something."

Marcus stared at her notes with the expression of someone studying a crime scene. "That's just... writing down chaos."

"Exactly," Isla said. "But here's the weird thing. Last year in history, I wrote the worst, most scattered notes about the French Revolution, right? Just fragments, random thoughts, Mrs. Patterson's jokes mixed in with actual dates. But when I studied them before the exam, something clicked. I could remember her saying something, and that helped me remember what she was talking about. It's like—" she paused, reaching for the right words, "—like I wasn't just recording information. I was recording the moment I was understanding it. So when I looked at my notes, I was kind of replaying my own thinking."

Marcus shifted in his seat, considering this. "So it's not about having perfect notes. It's about having notes that match how your brain actually processes things?"

"I mean, maybe," Isla said, pulling back slightly. She was aware she'd just claimed expertise in how brains work based on doing well on one test. "Or maybe I'm just lucky. But when I watch people who take those super clean, color-coded notes, they don't seem happier than me. They're not remembering more. They're just stressed about the formatting."

The bell rang—that actual bell, not the usual digital chime, because apparently the school district wanted to assault their students' eardrums on the first day. Teachers appeared in doorways like meerkats surveying the savanna. Marcus didn't move. He turned to a fresh page in his notebook and started writing the date, then looked at Isla. "You can," she said. "But don't tell anyone I gave you permission. I have no credentials whatsoever."

He grinned and wrote something she couldn't see, then underlined it twice, which she suspected wasn't actually necessary for any academic purpose but made him look committed. When he finished, he held it up like she'd just witnessed something momentous. It was indecipherable—a few incomplete sentences, a question mark, a small doodle of what might have been a sword or possibly a depressed spatula. It was thoroughly, beautifully useless to anyone but him.
